330.title: Greet Phoebe (Romans 16)
330.hook: the letter ends with a list of people, many of them women, like Phoebe the deacon
330.howItsDone: Many churches remember Phoebe, Priscilla and Junia among the saints and early leaders, and in most traditions deacons serve the poor, help in worship and care for the practical life of the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, proslambanesthe: the weak and the strong at one table. Your line was welcome one another.

Chapter sixteen of Romans looks like the credits at the end of a movie: a long list of names nobody can pronounce. Greet this one. Greet that one. Salute the household of so-and-so. Most people skip it. But stay for the credits: some of the best stories in the letter hide in that list. The very first name belongs to a woman traveling from a port town near Corinth, probably with the letter itself in her bag.
screen: `THE CREDITS AT THE END.` → `A LIST NOBODY READS.` → `THE FIRST NAME: A WOMAN WITH THE LETTER.`

segments.voice: Paul writes, in the King James Bible: "I commend unto you Phebe our sister, which is a servant of the church which is at Cenchrea." Cenchreae was the eastern port of Corinth. Servant here is diakonos, the root of deacon. Paul uses the same word for himself as a minister of the gospel, and even for Christ. Many scholars think Phoebe carried this letter to Rome, so she may have been the first to read it aloud there and answer questions about it. Paul asks the Romans to help her in whatever she needs, and calls her a helper, a patron, of many, and of Paul himself. Then the list. Priscilla and Aquila, a wife and husband who, Paul says, risked their necks for him, and who host a church in their home. Mary, who worked hard. Andronicus and Junia, who were in prison with Paul, and whom he calls of note among the apostles. Tryphaena and Tryphosa, two women who labor in the Lord. Rufus's mother, who, Paul says, was a mother to him too. More than two dozen names, around a third of them women. Even the secretary pops up: I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you. Churches today differ on women's roles. Many Protestant churches ordain women as deacons, and some as pastors. The early churches of the East had deaconesses, and some Orthodox churches are discussing restoring them. The Catholic Church ordains only men as deacons, and has been studying the question. But every church can read this list the same way: every name was a real someone.
screen: `PHOEBE, A DIAKONOS AT CENCHREAE.` · `SHE LIKELY CARRIED THE LETTER.` · `PRISCILLA, JUNIA, RUFUS'S MOTHER.` · `I TERTIUS, WHO WROTE THIS EPISTLE.` · then, large: `I COMMEND UNTO YOU PHEBE OUR SISTER.`

segments.voice: Think of the people who keep a place of faith or care running, whose names rarely get said: the person who sets up chairs, the one who runs the food pantry, a choir director, a janitor, a nursery volunteer, a chaplain; if you don't belong to a church, anyone who serves quietly, like a school secretary, a nurse or a crossing guard. Pick one and say their name to yourself, the way Paul does: greet this one. If you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Deacon. Diakonos in Greek: a servant, a minister. And Phoebe of Cenchreae, the first name in Paul's closing list, carries it.
Your line: every name is someone. That's the end of Romans. Tomorrow, the lookout over the year.

331.title: The big lookout
331.hook: from a carpenter's town to Rome, from a seed to a creed: look back at the hill you've climbed
331.howItsDone: Some Christians mark the end of a season or a year by looking back, giving thanks for what has passed before setting out again; in the Ignatian tradition a daily version of this is called the examen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Phoebe the deacon and the names at the end of Romans. Your line was every name is someone.

On a long trail there's a moment hikers talk about. Hours of looking down at boots: the next rock, the next root. Then the path opens onto a ledge, and you turn around. There it all is. The parking lot, tiny. The river you crossed. The steep bit that nearly made you quit. All of it, walked one step at a time. On day one you started at the bottom of this hill with one shared meal. Today is that ledge: skopos, the mark, and a look back at the whole climb before the path goes on.
screen: `HOURS OF LOOKING DOWN AT BOOTS.` → `THE PATH OPENS ONTO A LEDGE.` → `YOU TURN AROUND.`

segments.voice: Camp one was first words. Amen, a word you'd said a thousand times. Grace, a gift you didn't earn. The Lord's Prayer, one line a day: our Father, thy kingdom come, daily bread, forgive us, deliver us. Agape. The cross. Easter morning, and the women at the tomb first. Camp two was the stories: a sower flinging seed on every kind of ground, a father running down the road, a girl in Nazareth, a small carpenter's town, a road through Galilee, a last week in Jerusalem, then Acts, carrying the story to a shipwreck and to Rome. Camp three was the practices: ways to pray, Advent candles and the circle of the year, Sabbath, singing, giving, the sacraments, a rule of life. Camp four was Mark, read in order, breathless, from the first line to the empty tomb and the young man's words: he's going ahead of you to Galilee. Camp five went deep: the Sermon on the Mount, the mystics, the whole family of churches, the creeds that grew from that seed, and lately, Paul's letter to Rome. From a mustard seed to a creed. From prison, Paul wrote to his friends in Philippi, in the King James Bible: "forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before, I press toward the mark." The mark. The target. Remember hamartia, the word for sin that some readers hear as missing the mark? Paul's answer: don't stop aiming; keep pressing on. That's where year two begins: the whole Bible, in order, from its first line.
screen: `CAMP ONE: FIRST WORDS.` · `CAMPS TWO AND THREE: STORIES, PRACTICES.` · `CAMP FOUR: MARK, IN ORDER.` · `CAMP FIVE: THE DEPTHS, AND ROMANS.` · then, large: `I PRESS TOWARD THE MARK.`

segments.voice: Let the year pass in front of you like the view from the lookout, and find the line that stayed: one of the carries, like fear buries things, the story keeps going, no, not even that; a verse; or something you realized on your own, on an ordinary Tuesday. Not the most impressive one; the one that's actually yours. If you pray, give thanks for the climb so far.
Skopos. Paul's Greek word for the mark, the goal you keep your eyes on, pressing on past what's behind.
Your line: the hill goes on. You've walked every step of it. Day three hundred thirty-one.

332.title: In the beginning (Genesis 1:1–5)
332.hook: the earth without form, the Spirit over the waters, and the first word: let there be light
332.howItsDone: Bible-in-a-year plans start with Genesis 1, and some churches read it at the Easter Vigil, where the story of creation is one of the first readings of the night.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the big lookout, skopos: the whole first year behind you, and your line was the hill goes on.

The Bible doesn't open with a person. Before kings, prophets, a manger or a cross, there are three words in English: in the beginning. And the road starts somewhere strange: in the dark, over deep water, before there's anything to see at all. Year one walked the hill in pieces: words, stories, practices, one Gospel, the depths. Year two reads the whole book, in order, from the first line. Not every verse, but every turn of the road.
screen: `BEFORE KINGS, BEFORE PROPHETS.` → `YEAR TWO: THE WHOLE BOOK, IN ORDER.` → `IT STARTS IN THE DARK.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible the first verse reads: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." In Hebrew that opening phrase, in the beginning, is one word: bereshit. In Jewish tradition it's also the name of the whole book. Verse two sets the scene, and it isn't tidy: "And the earth was without form, and void; and darkness was upon the face of the deep." In Hebrew, tohu va-vohu, a pair of words that sound like a shrug. Waste and empty. But the same verse goes on: "And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters." The Hebrew word for Spirit, ruach, also means wind and breath. Some readers picture a bird hovering over a nest. Something is about to happen. And then, up close, the first thing we see God do is speak. "And God said, Let there be light: and there was light." No struggle, no battle, no raw material wrestled into shape. A word, and light. God calls the light day and the darkness night, and the evening and the morning are the first day. The strange part: the sun doesn't arrive until day four. Light comes before anything that shines. Christians have read this in many ways, from a literal week to a poem about order coming out of chaos, and churches hold different views on how it fits with the science of the universe. What they share is the opening claim: the world is made on purpose, by God. And Christians hear these words again at the start of John's Gospel: in the beginning was the Word.
screen: `BERESHIT: IN THE BEGINNING.` · `WITHOUT FORM, AND VOID.` · `THE SPIRIT OVER THE WATERS.` · `LIGHT BEFORE THE SUN.` · then, large: `LET THERE BE LIGHT.`

segments.voice: Notice where the light in this room is coming from: a window, a lamp, a screen. Close your eyes for a few breaths and rest in the dark behind your eyelids, then open them slowly and let the light come back in, as if for the first time. If you pray, say the first line of the Bible quietly; if not, just watch the light arrive.
Bereshit. The Hebrew word that opens the Bible and names its first book: in the beginning, before anything had form.
Your line: let there be light. A word first, and then everything else. Year two has begun.

333.title: Days of making (Genesis 1:6–25)
333.hook: sky, sea, land, plants, stars, fish, birds, animals, and after each: it was good
333.howItsDone: Some churches use the refrain of Genesis 1 in thanksgiving and creation-care services, and some keep a Season of Creation each September with readings from this chapter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bereshit, in the beginning: a dark deep, the Spirit over the waters, and your line was let there be light.

A carpenter steps back from a cabinet, runs a hand along the edge, and nods. A gardener looks down a row of seedlings, every one of them up. A kid holds up a drawing, still wet. That small pause, when someone makes a thing and then looks at it, runs all through the first chapter of the Bible. Day by day, the empty world fills: sky, sea, dry land, green things, lights, swimmers, fliers, creatures that creep and run. And after the making, again and again, God looks, and the same short sentence comes back.
screen: `A CARPENTER STEPS BACK AND NODS.` → `GOD MAKES, AND THEN GOD LOOKS.` → `THE SAME SHORT SENTENCE.`

segments.voice: Read the chapter slowly and a shape appears. The first three days make spaces. Day one, light and dark. Day two, a firmament, a great dome that splits the waters above from the waters below, and God calls it heaven. Day three, the waters gather, dry land appears, and the land brings forth grass and trees with seed in them. The next three days fill those spaces. Day four fills day and night with lights: "the greater light to rule the day, and the lesser light to rule the night: he made the stars also." The sun and moon aren't even named, just lights, with a job. Day five fills the sea and sky with fish and birds. Day six fills the land with animals, and with people, which is tomorrow. And after the making comes the line: "and God saw that it was good." In Hebrew, good is tov, the same word you'd use for a good meal or a good day. A small surprise: day two, the dome in the sky, is the one day where the Hebrew text doesn't say it was good. Readers have offered reasons; nobody knows for sure. Count the goods through the whole chapter, including the very good on day six, and you get seven. Christians read the days differently, some as six literal days, others as a poem with a pattern. Either way, the refrain is there to hear. Before anyone did anything right or wrong, the world was called good.
screen: `THREE DAYS MAKE SPACES.` · `THREE DAYS FILL THEM.` · `TOV: GOOD, LIKE A GOOD MEAL.` · `ONE DAY WITHOUT GOOD.` · then, large: `AND GOD SAW THAT IT WAS GOOD.`

segments.voice: Find one thing from the sky or the water, like a cloud or a glass of water; one green thing; and one living creature, a dog, a pigeon, a person you can hear in the next room. For each, pause the way the story does, look at it properly, and say quietly, it is good. If you pray, you can give thanks for each.
Tov. The Hebrew word for good, the refrain after each day of making: the same good used for a good meal.
Your line: and it was good. Seven times in one chapter, the same short sentence. See you tomorrow.

334.title: In his image (Genesis 1:26–31)
334.hook: humans made in God's image, male and female, and it was very good
334.howItsDone: Christian teaching on human dignity often starts from the image of God, and church statements cite Genesis 1:27 when speaking about the worth of every person, from the unborn to the dying, the poor and the stranger.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tov: spaces made, spaces filled, and your line was and it was good.

A carved stone king stands in a town square, weeks from his palace. Everyone who passes gets the message: this land is his, his authority reaches here. The image stands in for the king. Some scholars think the first hearers of today's verse would have known statues like that. Hold that picture. On the sixth day, after the land animals, the story slows down. God doesn't just say let there be. God says let us make. And what gets made is a creature that carries an image.
screen: `A KING'S STATUE IN A FAR-OFF TOWN.` → `THE RHYTHM CHANGES.` → `LET US MAKE.`

segments.voice: Here's verse twenty-seven in the King James Bible: "So God created man in his own image, in the image of God created he him; male and female created he them." The Hebrew word for image is tselem, used elsewhere in the Bible for a carved figure. In Latin, imago Dei, the image of God. Notice who's included: male and female, together, from the first line about people. Not a king, not a priest, not one special family. Every human. If those scholars are right, that's the twist: in Genesis, it isn't a ruler who carries God's image into the world. It's everyone. What the image actually is, the text doesn't spell out. Christians have suggested reason, or love, or the ability to make things, or the job in the next verse: to fill the earth and care for it as God's stand-ins. Some hold several at once. Another puzzle: let us make. Who is us? Some Christians, from early church writers on, hear a hint of the Trinity. Some Jewish commentators hear God speaking with the heavenly court. Others hear a plural of majesty, like a royal we. The text doesn't settle it. Then the chapter ends with God looking at everything one last time: "and, behold, it was very good." Not just good, like the other days. Very good. Christian traditions differ on what happened to the image after the garden. But Christians have used this verse to argue that no person can be owned, erased, or treated as nobody.

If you pray, you can give thanks for them.
Imago Dei. Latin for the image of God, the old claim from Genesis that every human, male and female, carries God's image.

335.title: Dust and breath (Genesis 2:4–7)
335.hook: the second telling: God shapes a human from the dust and breathes into its nose
335.howItsDone: On Ash Wednesday many Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran and Methodist Christians receive a cross of ashes on the forehead, often with words drawn from Genesis 3:19 about returning to dust.

segments.voice: Yesterday, imago Dei: every human made in God's image, and your line was very good.

Turn one page in Genesis and the story starts again. Chapter one told it from high above: days, lights, a world spoken into order, people made last. Chapter two drops down to the ground. No rain yet, no one to work the soil, just a mist coming up from the earth and watering it. And instead of speaking from a distance, God gets close. Hands in the dirt. The first chapter was a cathedral. The second is a workshop.
screen: `THE STORY STARTS AGAIN.` → `FROM HIGH ABOVE, THEN THE GROUND.` → `HANDS IN THE DIRT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul." Formed: the Hebrew verb is the one used for a potter shaping clay. Then a pun English loses. The ground is adamah. The human made from it is adam. Earthling from the earth. Adam isn't first a name here; it's a word for a human being, a creature of soil. Then the breath. God doesn't speak this one into being. God leans in and breathes into its nose, and the clay becomes a living soul, in Hebrew a nefesh, a living being. This telling differs from chapter one. The order changes, and even the name for God changes: chapter one says God, chapter two says the LORD God, the personal name. Many scholars think two older accounts were set side by side. Many Christians read them as two views of one event, a wide shot and a close-up. Either way, the book kept both. And the close-up says something about a person. You are dust, made of the same stuff as the ground under your shoes. And you are breath, given by God from close up. Not one or the other. In churches that keep Ash Wednesday, the ashes often go on with words from the next chapter: dust thou art. And many Christians link the breath with the Spirit; in both Hebrew and Greek, the word for spirit can also mean breath.

segments.voice: Feel your weight, your feet on the floor, your body heavy in the chair: that's the dust. Then breathe in slowly through your nose, five times, slower each time, and notice the air coming in: that's the breath. If you pray, you can give thanks for the breath you didn't have to make.
Adamah. The Hebrew word for ground, the soil a human, adam, was shaped from, then given breath to live.
Your line: dust with breath in it. Both halves, every day. Day three hundred thirty-five.

336.title: The garden and the names (Genesis 2:8–20)
336.hook: the human is set in a garden to tend it, and names the animals
336.howItsDone: Some Christians read Genesis 2:15 as a call to care for creation, and churches of several traditions hold creation-care services, community gardens and blessings of animals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, adamah: a human shaped from the ground and given breath, and your line was dust with breath in it. Today ends the week.

What was Adam's first job? Before any fruit, any serpent, any fall, Genesis gives the first human work. Not a throne. A garden. Somewhere in the east, the story says, God plants it, with every tree pleasant to look at and good for food, and a river running out of it that splits into four. One, the Euphrates, is still on the map today, and another, Hiddekel, is usually taken to be the Tigris. And the first person in the Bible is put to work as a gardener, and asked to name the animals.
screen: `ADAM'S FIRST JOB?` → `A GARDEN, PLANTED IN THE EAST.` → `A RIVER STILL ON THE MAP.`

segments.voice: The garden's name is Eden. In Hebrew it sounds like a word for delight, or luxury. When the Bible was put into Greek, the translators called this garden a paradeisos, a word for a park. That's where English gets paradise. But the verse that matters most today is fifteen, in the King James Bible: "And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it." Two Hebrew verbs. The first, avad, means to work, to serve; it's the word used later for serving God in worship. The second, shamar, means to keep, to guard, to watch over; the same word is used later for keeping God's commandments. So the first human job is to serve the ground and guard it. Christians have read this verse in different ways over the centuries, some stressing the human as ruler of creation, others, more recently, the human as caretaker. Then God brings every animal to the man, "to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof." God doesn't hand out a list. God waits to see. Naming, in this story, is how a human pays attention. And so ends a week that began on a lookout and went back to the very beginning: light, good, image, dust and breath, and now a garden to tend.
screen: `EDEN: DELIGHT, A PARADISE.` · `TO DRESS IT AND TO KEEP IT.` · `SERVE THE GROUND, GUARD IT.` · `GOD WAITS TO SEE THE NAMES.` · then, large: `THAT WAS THE NAME THEREOF.`

segments.voice: Think of a living thing you pass all the time without knowing its name: the tree outside your window, the weed in the sidewalk crack, the small brown bird on the wire. Picture its shape, its color, where it lives, and give it a few breaths of real attention. If you pray, you can give thanks for it.
Eden. A Hebrew name that sounds like delight. A garden planted in the east, where the first human was given work: to serve it and to guard it.
Your line: tend and keep. The first job was a gardener's. A week of beginnings, done.
